description: How businesses are structured, how people communicate, and flexible working.
content_html:
What Is an Organisational Structure?

As a business grows beyond a handful of people, it needs to decide how authority and responsibility are arranged. An organisational structure shows who reports to whom, how decisions are made, and how many layers of management exist between the top and bottom of the business.

The two most common structures studied at GCSE are hierarchical structures and flat structures. The right choice depends on the size of the business, its culture, and how quickly it needs to make decisions.

Hierarchical Structures

A hierarchical structure has many levels of management stacked on top of each other like a pyramid. At the top sit directors, then senior managers, then supervisors, and finally operational staff at the base. Each person manages a small number of people — this is called a narrow span of control.

Large organisations such as supermarket chains often use hierarchical structures because clear lines of authority help manage thousands of employees across many locations. Instructions travel down the chain of command and feedback travels upward. This makes coordination easier — everyone knows exactly who their manager is and who they are responsible for.

The disadvantage is that communication can become slow and distorted as messages pass through many layers. Employees at the bottom may feel disempowered if all decisions are taken far above them. This is a feature of centralised hierarchies, where senior leaders hold most of the power.

Key Fact

In a hierarchical structure, there are many layers, a narrow span of control, and a long chain of command. Communication tends to be slow but roles and responsibilities are very clear. It suits large, well-established businesses with standardised processes.

Flat Structures

A flat structure removes most of the middle management layers. Each manager oversees a large number of employees — a wide span of control. This means messages reach decision-makers faster, and employees are often given more responsibility and autonomy.

Many technology start-ups and creative agencies use flat structures because they encourage rapid decision-making and collaboration. However, when the business grows, managers can become overstretched if they are responsible for too many people at once. A wide span of control only works well when employees are highly skilled and need little supervision.

Organisational structure connects closely to where decisions are made. In a centralised structure, key decisions are taken by senior managers at the top. This keeps tight control and consistency across a large business — every branch of a franchise, for example, follows the same rules. The risk is that senior managers become overloaded and may be too remote from customers to make the best choices.

In a decentralised structure, authority is delegated to managers or teams lower down or at regional levels. Local managers can respond more quickly to customer needs, and employees tend to feel more motivated when they have genuine decision-making power. The downside is that standards can become inconsistent across different parts of the business.

Communication in Organisations

Effective communication is essential for any business. When employees receive clear, accurate, and timely information, they can do their jobs well and feel part of the organisation. Poor communication creates confusion, lowers morale, and wastes time.

However, there can be too much of a good thing. Excessive communication — endless meetings, constant email chains, multiple sign-off chains — slows down operations and frustrates employees just as much as insufficient communication does. Businesses need to find the right balance.

Several things can prevent a message from being understood correctly. Physical barriers include noise, poor internet connections, or employees working in different time zones. Jargon and overly technical language can confuse people who are not specialists. Too many layers in the chain of command mean messages can be altered or misunderstood as they pass through each level. Cultural differences between team members may cause misinterpretation of tone or meaning. Overloaded managers may simply fail to pass information along at all. Businesses can reduce these barriers by using clear language, choosing the right communication channel (email, face-to-face, video call), and keeping their structure as lean as is practical.

Key Fact

Both too little and too much communication harm efficiency and motivation. Too little leaves employees uninformed; too much overloads them with irrelevant messages. The structure of the organisation itself can be a barrier — longer chains of command increase the chance of distortion.

Ways of Working

Businesses do not employ everyone on the same terms. The way work is organised affects costs, flexibility, and employee wellbeing. There are several key distinctions:

Full-time employees work a standard working week. Part-time employees work a reduced number of hours. Part-time contracts give businesses flexibility to match staffing levels to demand — useful in retail during evenings and weekends — while reducing wage costs. For employees, part-time work can improve work–life balance but may offer fewer career development opportunities.

Flexible hours arrangements allow employees to vary their start and finish times around core hours. This can increase motivation and reduce absenteeism, but requires careful management so that adequate staffing levels are maintained at all times.

Businesses also choose between permanent contracts and temporary contracts. Permanent staff offer continuity and loyalty; temporary workers give the business flexibility to scale up during busy periods without long-term commitment. Some workers are hired as freelancers — self-employed specialists brought in on a project basis. A graphic designer hired to create a new logo, for example, would typically be a freelancer.

Technology has transformed how and where work takes place. Remote working became widespread after advances in cloud software, video conferencing, and secure file-sharing. For businesses, remote working can reduce office costs and widen the pool of available talent beyond a single city. For employees, it can improve work–life balance and cut commuting time.

However, remote working also creates challenges. Collaboration can be harder when teams are spread across locations. Managers find it more difficult to monitor performance, and newer employees may struggle to learn informally from colleagues. Businesses need clear communication systems and performance targets to make remote working effective rather than simply convenient.
exam_tip_html: On a 6-mark Explain question about organisational structures, you only need two well-developed points — the examiner credits the best two only. A safe approach: state your point clearly, then give two linked expansion sentences. For example: “A flat structure has a wide span of control. This means each manager oversees more employees, which can reduce wage costs by employing fewer managers. However, if managers are overstretched, supervision quality may fall, leading to mistakes and lower quality.” Note that no case-study context is needed for Explain questions — adding one doesn’t earn extra marks. For 9-mark Discuss questions, you must weigh up more than one point of view and refer to relevant business concepts throughout. Avoid listing advantages and disadvantages in separate blocks — the best answers interweave evidence, analysis, and judgement throughout.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hierarchical structures have many layers and a narrow span of control, giving clear roles and authority but slow communication; flat structures have fewer layers and a wider span of control, enabling faster decisions but risking overstretched managers.
  • Centralised businesses concentrate decision-making at the top for consistency and control; decentralised businesses delegate authority to local managers for faster responses and greater employee motivation.
  • Businesses choose between full-time, part-time, flexible, permanent, temporary, and freelance contracts to balance cost and flexibility; technology has enabled remote working, reducing overheads while creating new communication challenges.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a flat organisational structure?
A) Many layers of management with a narrow span of control
B) Few layers of management with a wide span of control
C) Decision-making concentrated at the top of the business
D) A structure used only by public limited companies
practice_questions.marks: B) Few layers of management with a wide span of control [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two benefits to a business of using part-time rather than full-time contracts.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each for any two of the following (no development required):
• Lower wage costs / smaller wage bill
• Greater flexibility to match staffing to demand
• Easier to scale workforce up or down during busy / quiet periods
• Reduced cost of employee benefits (e.g. pension contributions)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline one advantage and one disadvantage of a decentralised organisational structure.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantage (1 mark for identification + 1 mark for brief development linked to context):
• Decision-making is delegated to local managers, who can respond quickly to customer needs in their area — decisions are made by those closest to the situation. [1+1]

Disadvantage (1 mark):
• Inconsistency can develop across different parts of the business if local managers make different decisions about processes, pricing or quality. [1]
[3 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why effective communication is important for a growing business.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark the best two points only. Up to 3 marks per point: 1 mark for a relevant statement, plus up to 2 marks for developed explanation.

Point 1 example:
• Effective communication ensures employees understand their roles and targets. [1] When all staff know what is expected of them, they can carry out tasks correctly the first time, reducing errors and improving efficiency. [+1] This is especially important in a growing business where new employees are joining regularly and need clear guidance to perform well quickly. [+1]

Point 2 example:
• Good communication reduces the risk of costly mistakes. [1] If managers fail to pass on changes to procedures or specifications, operational staff may continue working in the wrong way, producing defective goods or providing incorrect information to customers. [+1] This can damage the business's reputation and result in lost sales that are expensive to recover. [+1]

Other creditable points: boosts employee motivation / reduces conflict / supports coordination across departments.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Harrow Peak Kitchens is a growing bespoke kitchen manufacturer based in Leeds. The business currently employs 85 people across two sites. The founder, Elena Harrow, manages all key decisions herself — from supplier negotiations to staffing and marketing. Senior managers have told her they feel unable to act without her approval, which is slowing down responses to customers. Elena is considering whether to change to a more decentralised structure.

Discuss whether a decentralised structure would benefit Harrow Peak Kitchens.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): A sustained discussion that analyses the benefits of decentralisation in the context of a growing, two-site business (faster customer response, motivated managers with real authority) AND examines potential drawbacks (risk of inconsistent standards across sites, Elena may need to invest in management training before delegating). The answer reaches a supported judgement about whether decentralisation is likely to benefit this specific business, referencing Elena's current bottleneck problem and the two-site context.

Secure (5–7 marks): The answer explores at least two relevant points — for example, that decentralisation speeds up decision-making and that Elena is currently a bottleneck — with some development and reference to the case. Judgement is present but may lack full supporting reasoning.

Developing (3–4 marks): Some relevant points about decentralisation are made but they may be one-sided or insufficiently developed. Limited use of the case-study context. A basic conclusion may be present.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Simple statements about centralisation or decentralisation with little or no development or reference to Harrow Peak Kitchens.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Westbridge Media is a creative agency in Bristol with 40 employees. The business is currently structured as a hierarchy with five layers of management. Staff have complained that ideas take too long to reach decision-makers, and several talented employees have left because they felt their work was too tightly controlled. The managing director is considering whether to move to a flat structure or to retain the hierarchy but decentralise decision-making.

Justify one recommendation for how Westbridge Media should restructure its organisation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): A fully developed recommendation — either flat structure or decentralised hierarchy — with strong reasoning linked to Westbridge Media's specific problems (staff turnover due to over-control, slow idea flow, 40 employees in a creative industry). The student justifies why the recommended option is better than the alternative, acknowledges at least one limitation of their choice, and reaches a clear, contextualised conclusion.

Secure (7–9 marks): A clear recommendation with developed reasoning and some reference to the case. The contrast with the alternative option may be present but less fully argued. A conclusion is reached.

Developing (4–6 marks): A recommendation is made but justification is partially developed. Limited reference to Westbridge Media's context. The alternative option may be briefly mentioned.

Emerging (1–3 marks): A recommendation is identified but little or no justification is offered. Minimal or no use of the case-study context.
[12 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which organisational structure has the most layers of management?
What is the span of control in an organisation?
options: The number of products a manager is responsible for
The range of decisions a manager can make
The number of employees directly managed by one person
The distance between head office and regional branches

knowledge_checks.q: In a _____ structure, decision-making authority is spread across different levels or locations rather than being concentrated at the top.
A _____ worker is self-employed and contracted to complete a specific task or project without being a permanent employee.
Match each working arrangement to its definition:
right: A standard working week, typically 35–40 hours
A fixed-period contract that ends after a set time or project
Working from a location away from the employer's main premises

flashcard_questions.a: The system defining how roles, authority and responsibilities are coordinated within a business.

flashcard_questions.q: What does span of control mean?
flashcard_questions.a: The number of employees directly managed by one person.

flashcard_questions.q: In a hierarchical structure, is the span of control narrow or wide?
flashcard_questions.a: Narrow — each manager oversees only a few people across many layers.

flashcard_questions.q: In a flat structure, is the span of control narrow or wide?
flashcard_questions.a: Wide — each manager oversees many people across very few layers.
Key decisions are made by senior leaders at the top of the organisation.
Authority is delegated to managers or teams at lower or regional levels.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one advantage of a flat structure over a hierarchical one.
flashcard_questions.a: Faster communication and decision-making due to fewer management layers.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one disadvantage of a flat structure.
flashcard_questions.a: Managers can become overstretched if responsible for too many employees.

flashcard_questions.q: How does too many layers in a hierarchy affect communication?
flashcard_questions.a: Messages can be distorted or delayed as they pass through each level.
A self-employed worker contracted for specific tasks, not employed by the business.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might a business use part-time rather than full-time contracts?
flashcard_questions.a: To reduce wage costs and match staffing levels to fluctuating demand.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one business benefit of allowing remote working.
flashcard_questions.a: Reduced office costs and access to a wider pool of talent beyond one location.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one challenge of remote working for a business.
flashcard_questions.a: Harder for managers to monitor performance and for teams to collaborate informally.

glossary_terms.definition: The system that defines how activities, roles and responsibilities are coordinated within a business.
An organisational structure with multiple layers of management, a narrow span of control, and a clear chain of command from top to bottom.
The number of employees directly managed by one person.
A structure in which decision-making authority is concentrated at the top levels of the organisation.
An organisational structure with few layers of management, a wide span of control, and shorter lines of communication.
A structure in which decision-making authority is spread across different levels or locations within the organisation.
Work arranged into regular hours across all working days of the week, typically 35–40 hours.
Work arranged for fewer hours or days than a standard full working week.
A contract that does not fix working hours in advance; the employer offers work and the employee can accept or decline.
A long-term employment contract with no set end date, providing job security.
A contract for a fixed period or specific project, after which employment ends unless renewed.
Self-employed workers contracted to complete specific tasks or projects, without being employees of the business.
Working from a location other than the employer's main premises, typically from home, enabled by digital technology.
